q: The Silver Rupiya, which remained a standard currency for centuries was introduced by
explanation: The silver rupiya of about 178 grains, which remained the standard coin for centuries, was introduced by Sher Shah Suri (1540-45).

notes.text: - Managed his father's jagir from **1511**; joined **Bahar Khan** of Bihar, who gave him the title **"Sher Khan"** for killing a **tiger**.

q:
Consider the following statements on Sher Shah's land revenue administration:
I. Land was classified into three categories on the basis of produce from the land.
II. Land was measured according to a uniform system.
III. 1/4 of the produce was collected as tax.
Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sher Shah measured land by a uniform system (gaz-i-Sikandari) and classified it into three categories (good, middling, bad) by produce, so I and II are correct. The state's share was one-third, not one-fourth, so III is wrong.

notes.text: - **APPSC G1 PYQ:** three categories – TRUE; uniform measurement – TRUE; "1/4 collected" – FALSE → **I and II**. ⚠ NextGen writes "one fourth or one third"; the standard books (Satish Chandra) give **one-third**.

q: The rate of land tax levied by Shershah was
explanation: Sher Shah fixed the state's share at one-third of the average produce, after measuring the land and classing it into three grades.

notes.text: - **Rate of land tax: 1/3 of produce** (APPSC G1 2012) – not 1/4, 1/2 or 1/5.

q: At the time of his coronation at Kalanaur the age Lat par The of Akbar was:
explanation:
Most books and keys: fourteen. Strictly, born 15 Oct 1542 and crowned 14 Feb 1556, he was 13 years 4 months (Rocket: 'age <14').
Akbar was crowned at Kalanaur in February 1556 at about fourteen (NextGen: 'only fourteen years old'), so 'fourteen' is the intended answer; fifteen, eighteen and twenty are wrong.

notes.text: - **Abul Fazl's death** was caused by **Prince Salim** (Jharkhand 2013); actual killer **Bir Singh Deo Bundela** (MPSC 2009) – not Hemu, Bairam Khan or Udai Singh.

q: During whose reign did the Mughal empire become a political fact and a factor in the life of India, influencing her ever since?
explanation: Under Akbar's long reign (1556-1605) the Mughal empire was consolidated by conquest, mansabdari and Rajput policy and became a lasting political fact in India.

q: Name the Rana of Mewar who employed Baksariya Muslims in his army :
explanation: The APPSC key names Maharana Pratap, whose army against the Mughals also included Muslim troops (Hakim Khan Sur's Afghans); Kumbha, Udai Singh and Raj Singh are not linked with the Baksariyas.

notes.text: - Rana Pratap employed **Baksariya Muslims** in his army (APPSC G1 2019 key).

q: Among the following, who was the illiterate?
explanation: Akbar was unlettered, though he created conditions for learning; Aurangzeb, Jahangir and Babur were literate (Babur and Jahangir wrote memoirs).

notes.text: - **Akbar was unlettered (illiterate)** but a great patron of learning (APPSC G2 2011) – Babur, Jahangir and Aurangzeb were literate.

exam: APPSC Teaching Staff of the Department of Technical Educatio
q: The Mansabdari system was introduced by?
explanation: The mansabdari system was introduced by Akbar (dagh 1573-74, zat-sawar ranks 1595-96); Jahangir only added du-aspa sih-aspa.

q: The "Dahsala" system developed by Raja Todar Mal was for
options: Collection of land revenue at standard rate which was valid for 10 years
Measurement of land once in 10 years for fixing area of assessment
Collection of revenue on the basis of average of produce and prices in the last 10 years
Sharing of crop between the farmer and the State for 10 years
key_text: Collection of revenue on the basis of average of produce and prices in the last 10 years
explanation: The Dahsala (1580) fixed revenue on the average produce and prices of the previous ten years (1571-80), converted into cash - not a fixed ten-year rate or a ten-yearly survey.

notes.text: - **Dahsala = collection of revenue on the average of produce and prices of the last 10 years** (APPSC G2 2017) – NOT a fixed 10-year rate, a 10-yearly measurement, or a 10-year crop-sharing deal.

q: In medieval Deccan, Deshmukh was a village official, wh responsible to-
options: Collect land revenue from the peasants and to deposit it in the State treasury
Maintain law and order in the village
key_text: Collect land revenue from the peasants and to deposit it in the State treasury
explanation: The Deshmukh, a hereditary Deccan officer over a pargana, collected land revenue from the peasants and deposited it in the state treasury.

notes.text: - **Deshmukh** (medieval Deccan): **collected land revenue** from the peasants and deposited it in the state treasury (APPSC G1) – a hereditary watandar over a pargana.

q:
Match the following revenue officials during the reign of Akbar with their duties:
List I
List II
a. Amalguzar
I. Kept records of the revenue payable by the villages
b. Karkuns
II. Revenue Collector in-charge of a District
c. Qanungo
III. Accountant
d. Bitikchi
IV. Prepared the seasonal crop statistics
explanation: Amalguzar - district revenue collector (II), Karkuns - crop statistics (IV), Qanungo - village revenue records (I), Bitikchi - accountant (III): a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III; only option b has the amalguzar right.

notes.text: - **APPSC G1 match:** Amalguzar–district revenue collector (II), Karkuns–crop statistics (IV), Qanungo–village revenue records (I), Bitikchi–accountant (III) = **a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III**.

q:
Which of the following incidents took place during the reign of Jahangir?
I. The fifth Sikh Guru, Arjan Dev was sentenced to death.
II. Victory over Rajputs of Mewar.
III. Annexation of Kabul and Kandahar.
IV. Arrival of English East India Company to India.
explanation: Guru Arjan Dev's execution (1606), Mewar's submission (1615) and the English arrival (Hawkins 1608, Roe 1615) all fall in Jahangir's reign. Kandahar was lost by Jahangir in 1622, not annexed, so III is wrong.

notes.text: - **Capital shifted from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi), 1638-48**; Red Fort, Jama Masjid, **Taj Mahal** (for Mumtaz – not Jodha Bai or Nur Jahan); **Peacock Throne** (taken by **Nadir Shah, 1739**); reign = "golden age" of architecture.

q: What was the childhood name of Nur Jahan?
explanation:
Printed APPSC key: Bahu Begam. Verified: Mehr-un-Nisa (NextGen, PMF, Britannica).
Nur Jahan was born Mehr-un-Nisa (Mehrunnisa; 'Maharul Nisa' here), daughter of Mirza Ghiyas Beg. 'Bahu Begam' in the printed APPSC key is not her name in any standard source, and Mumtaz was Arjumand Banu's title.

q: Who was known as the Plato of the Jat tribe?
explanation: Maharaja Suraj Mal of Bharatpur (r. 1755-63) was called 'the Plato of the Jat tribe' by a contemporary historian for his political wisdom.

q: Which Mughal emperor captured the kingdom of Golconda in 1687?
explanation: Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687.

notes.text: - Titles of royal women: **Roshanara = Padshah Begum**; **Jahanara = Sahibat-uz-Zamani**.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Mughal Empire (AD 1526 - AD 1857):

1. The Mughal Empire was established by Babur after his victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

2. Akbar introduced the Mansabdari system to organize the administration and the army.

3. Aurangzeb was known for his patronage of arts and architecture, especially building the Taj Mahal.

4. The decline of the Mughal Empire began after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; 3 is wrong because the Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan, not Aurangzeb.

notes.text: - **Statements (APPSC ASO):** Babur founded the empire at **Panipat 1526**; Akbar's mansabdari; decline after **1707** – but the **Taj Mahal was Shah Jahan's**, not Aurangzeb's.

q: Who was the 17th-century French traveller who visited the mines of Andhra in search of fine gems and diamonds?
explanation: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a French gem merchant, visited the Golconda diamond mines (Kollur) in the 17th century. Bernier, Thevenot and Manucci are not linked with the mines.

q:
Match the following books with their authors:
List I
List II
a. India at the Death of Akbar 1. Irfan Habib
b. The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707 II. François Bernier
c. Travels in the Mogul Empire : AD 1656-1668 III. William Foster
d. Early Travels in India, 1583-1619 IV. Moreland
explanation: Moreland wrote India at the Death of Akbar, Irfan Habib The Agrarian System of Mughal India, Bernier the Travels in the Mogul Empire, and Foster edited Early Travels in India: a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III.

q: The Venetian who came to India at 16, served as answer and answer the questions: an artilleryman with Dara Shikoh, and left lengthy memoirs about India, was:
explanation: Niccolao Manucci, a Venetian, came to India at about 16, served as an artilleryman with Dara Shikoh and wrote the Storia do Mogor.

q: Travernier who visited Andhra during the Qutub Shahi dynasty was a traveler of which country?
explanation: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a French jeweller who visited Golconda's diamond mines under the Qutb Shahis.

q: The class of traders who specialized in carrying bulk goods over long distances during Mughal period were called
explanation: Banjaras carried bulk goods like grain and salt over long distances in bullock caravans. Baniks and Beoparis were local traders and Sarrafs bankers.

q: In Mughal period, the letter of credit issued by Shroffs (money keepers) to people who deposited cash for collecting it later or collecting the cash at a different place after journey was called?
explanation: A hundi was a letter of credit issued by shroffs against deposited cash, encashable later or at another place. A farman is a royal order and rokad means cash.

notes.text: - **Hundi** – **letter of credit** issued by shroffs against deposited cash; encashed later or at another place – not Farman (royal order), Parcha, Rokad (cash). **Bima** – insurance of goods in transit.

q: During Mughal period, approximately how much percentage of rural agricultural produce was marketed?
explanation:
Printed PYQ keys: 15%. The app's old notes (and own MCQ g6f7cea038e5f) said 25% was the APPSC G2 2017 key; no library source settles it.
The printed key in both copies of this APPSC G2 2017 question is about 15%. The app's old notes gave 25% as the key; the figure is not stated in the library or standard books.

notes.text: - **Marketed share:** about **15%** of rural agricultural produce (APPSC G2 2017, printed key in both PYQ copies) – the old app notes gave **25%**; disputed, see the PYQ note. Cash revenue pushed peasants to sell.

q: What is the dowry for a Muhammadan bride called?
explanation: Mehr is the dower that a Muslim bridegroom pays or promises to the bride under sharia; it is her own property. Stridhana is the Hindu woman's property.

notes.text: - **Property:** Muslim women – inheritance shares + **mehr** (the dower a Muslim bridegroom pays the bride, APPSC 2000) under sharia; Hindu women – **stridhana**.

q:
Consider the following Mughal structures:
I. Tomb of Salim Chishti
II. Buland Darwaza
III. Tomb of Humayun
IV. Jami Masjid
Which of the above buildings were constructed during the reign of Akbar?
explanation: All four belong to Akbar's reign: the Jama Masjid, Buland Darwaza and Salim Chishti's tomb at Fatehpur Sikri, and Humayun's tomb (1565-72), built by Haji Begum under Akbar.

notes.text: - **Built in Akbar's reign (APPSC G1):** Tomb of Salim Chishti, Buland Darwaza, Jami Masjid (Fatehpur Sikri) **and** Humayun's Tomb (1565–72) – **all four**.

q: Who built the tomb of Itimal-ud-daula at Agra?
explanation: Nur Jahan built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra (1622-28) for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg; Jahangir was the reigning emperor, not the builder.

q: What is the method used by ASI to remove superficial spots on marble of Taj Mahal?
explanation: The ASI cleans the Taj's yellowed marble with a 'mud pack' of fuller's earth (multani mitti), left on and washed off – the mud-pack therapy. Chlorine bleach and abrasives would damage the marble.

notes.text: - **Conservation:** ASI removes surface stains with a **mud pack** of fuller's earth (**multani mitti**) – "mud pack therapy" – not chlorine bleaching or abrasives.

q: Which of the following places was the major source of marble used for construction of Taj Mahal?
explanation: The Taj's white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan. Kishangarh and Rajnagar are later marble centres.

q: In how many volume Abul Fazl wrote a history of Akbar’s reign, titled Akbar Nama?
explanation: The Akbarnama has three volumes: Akbar's ancestors, Akbar's reign, and the Ain-i-Akbari.

q: In the Hindu-Muslim composite culture of medieval India, the long-necked Persian lute was combined with the classical Indian veena to form the:
explanation: The sitar combines the Persian long-necked lute (setar) with the Indian veena, a product of Indo-Persian musical synthesis.

notes.text: - **Not illustrated at Akbar's court (CDS 2016 key): Tarikh-i-Alfi** – a textual chronicle; Hamzanama, Razmnama and Baburnama copies were richly painted (a few Alfi folios did carry pictures).

q: The style of vocal Hindustani music which was non-Islamic in character was:
explanation:
Keys: Dhrupad. The app's old notes say an APPSC key gave 'Taraka' (not a recognised style); Dhrupad is the verified answer.
Dhrupad, the oldest Hindustani vocal form, is devotional and indigenous (non-Islamic) in character, unlike Khayal and Qawwali (Persian/Sufi-influenced); 'Taraka' is not a recognised vocal style.

q: What was the original name of Tanson?
explanation: Tansen's original name was Ramtanu Pande (also called Tanna Mishra); Baz Bahadur was the Malwa sultan-musician.

q: Who of the following translated the Bhagavad Gita into Persian? B) Ghalib
explanation: Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's eldest son, translated the Bhagavad Gita, the Upanishads and the Yoga Vasistha into Persian; Ghalib was a 19th-century Urdu poet.

notes.text: - UPSC 2012 Dhrupad: 1 (originated in Rajput kingdoms during the Mughal period) is **wrong**; 2 and 3 are right → **2 and 3**.

q: Identify the correct chronology of Later Mughals:
options: Bahadur Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Jahandar Shah > Muhammad Shah > Shah Alam-II
Bahadur Shah Jahandar Shah > Muhammad Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Shah Alam-II
Bahadur Shah Jahandar Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Muhammad Shah > Shah Alam-II
Farrukh Siyar > Jahandar Shah > Muhammad Shah Shah Alam-II > Bahadur Shah
key_text: Bahadur Shah Jahandar Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Muhammad Shah > Shah Alam-II
explanation: The order of reigns is Bahadur Shah I (1707-12), Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Farrukhsiyar (1713-19), Muhammad Shah (1719-48) and Shah Alam II (1759-1806). The other options swap Farrukhsiyar and Muhammad Shah or put Bahadur Shah last.

notes.text: - **Order (APPSC G1, UPPSC 2018, UPRO 2023):** **Bahadur Shah I → Jahandar Shah → Farrukhsiyar → Muhammad Shah → Ahmad Shah → Alamgir II → Shah Alam II**.

q: Who founded the Hyderabad State?
options: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)
key_text: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)
explanation:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)); it is added as option 5.
Hyderabad State (the Asaf Jahi dominion) was founded by Chin Qilich Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, in 1724, and none of the printed names is he. Quli Qutb Shah founded only Hyderabad city (1591), and Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were later claimants.

notes.text: - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).

q: When was Hyderabad State established?
explanation: Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda in 1724 and became virtually independent, so 1724 is Hyderabad State's founding year.

notes.text: - **1724:** defeated the Mughal governor **Mubariz Khan** at **Shakar Kheda** → virtually independent. **Died 1748** (APPSC G2 1993, MPDO 1997).

q: Give the name of founder of the state of Hyderabad:
explanation: Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the state of Hyderabad in 1724. Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were his successors and rivals after 1748, and Zulfiqar Khan only envisaged the Deccan state.

notes.text: - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).

notes.text: - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).

q: Who was the founder of the Asaf Jahi dynasty in the Deccan?
explanation: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724. Salar Jung was a 19th-century minister and Nizam Ali the second Nizam.

notes.text: - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).

q: Who was the founder of the Asaf Jahi Dynasty in the Deccan?
explanation: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda.

notes.text: - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).

q: The first Nizam of Hyderabad, who accepted Lord Wellesley's plan of Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, was
explanation: Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II, 1762-1803) accepted Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, the first ruler to do so. Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam and Nizam-ul-Mulk the first.

q: Who was the last Asaf Jahi (Nizam) ruler?
explanation: Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911-48), founder of Osmania University, was the seventh and last Asaf Jahi Nizam. Afzal-ud-Daula and Mahbub Ali Khan came earlier.

q: Asaf Jahi dynasty was founded in which year?
explanation: Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724; 1748 is the year he died.

notes.text: - **1724:** defeated the Mughal governor **Mubariz Khan** at **Shakar Kheda** → virtually independent. **Died 1748** (APPSC G2 1993, MPDO 1997).

q: In which year did Nizam ul Mulk die?
explanation: Nizam-ul-Mulk ruled from 1724 until his death in 1748.

notes.text: - **1724:** defeated the Mughal governor **Mubariz Khan** at **Shakar Kheda** → virtually independent. **Died 1748** (APPSC G2 1993, MPDO 1997).

explanation: Murshid Quli Khan, Diwan (1700) and then Nazim of Bengal, introduced revenue farming (ijaradari). Alivardi Khan, Sarfaraz Khan and Siraj-ud-Daulah came later.

q: Out of the following, who plundered Delhi and carried away the Koh-i-Noor diamond?
explanation: Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried away the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne. Abdali and Timur are the tempting wrong options.

q: In medieval Deccan, Deshmukh was a village official, who was responsible to
options: Collect land revenue from the peasants and to deposit it in the State treasury
Collect chauth from the local chiefs
key_text: Collect land revenue from the peasants and to deposit it in the State treasury
explanation: The Deshmukh, a hereditary pargana-level official of the Deccan, collected land revenue from the peasants for the state treasury. Chauth was a Maratha levy, not his duty.

q: ______ looked after finance during the reign of Shivaji.
explanation: The Amatya (Majumdar) was Shivaji's finance minister. The Sachiv handled correspondence, and Sar-i-Naubat was the army commander.

q: In Shivaji's administration, Dabir was:
options: An officer responsible for intelligence, posts and household affairs
The in-charge of justice and charitable grants
The Master of Ceremonies and helped the king in foreign affairs
key_text: The Master of Ceremonies and helped the king in foreign affairs
explanation: The Dabir (Sumant) was the master of ceremonies who helped the king in foreign affairs and received envoys. Intelligence belonged to the Mantri, justice to the Nyayadhish, and correspondence to the Sachiv.

q: Among Ashtapradhans of Shivaji, the Sar-i-Naubat was associated with which of the following tasks?
explanation: Sar-i-Naubat was the Persian title of the Senapati, the military commander. Finance belonged to the Amatya and foreign affairs to the Sumant.

q: In which fort was Shivaji born in 1630?
explanation: Shivaji was born in 1630 at the hill fort of Shivneri near Pune. Raigad was his capital and coronation fort, and Sinhagad (Kondana) was a later conquest.

notes.text: - **Born at Shivneri fort** near Pune, **19 February 1630** (Maharashtra government date; PMF); Jadunath Sarkar's **1627** gives the key "**1627, 1674**" (UPPCS 2015). Parents **Shahaji Bhonsle and Jijabai**; **Dadaji Kondadev** = keeper of the **Pune jagir** and tutor.

q: The spiritual guru of Shivaji was
explanation: Samarth Ramdas, author of the Dasbodh, is regarded as Shivaji's spiritual guru. Eknath died in 1599, before Shivaji was born, and Namdev was a 14th-century saint (official key printed: Eknath).

notes.text: - **Guru:** **Samarth Ramdas** (Dasbodh, Shivastuti); saint contemporary **Tukaram**. Ramdas, not Eknath (died 1599), is the APPSC G1 2012 answer.

q: The first port occupied by Shivaji was:
explanation: Torna (1646), taken from Bijapur when Shivaji was 16, was the first fort he captured (the stem's 'port' means fort). Purandar, Kondana and Raigad came later.

q: Shivaji signed the Treaty of 'Purandhar' in which year and with whom?
explanation: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed with the Mughal general Raja Jai Singh of Amber. Shivaji killed Afzal Khan in 1659 and raided Shaista Khan in 1663.

q: Who among the following had assumed the title of 'Haindava Dharmoddharak'?
explanation: At his 1674 coronation Shivaji took the titles 'Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati' and 'Haindava Dharmoddharak'. Shahu and the Peshwas came later.

notes.text: - **Coronation:** priest **Gaga Bhatt** (Vishweshwar) of Banaras; titles "**Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati**" and **Haindava Dharmoddharak** (not "Hindavi Sultan"); era **Rajyabhisheka Shaka**.

q: Third Battle of Panipat was fought between
options: Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Madho Rao Scindia
Ahmad Shah Abdali and the Marathas

q: Which was the seat of power of Peshwas?
explanation: The Peshwas ruled from Poona (Pune); Balaji Baji Rao shifted the government there after Shahu's death. Nagpur was the Bhonsle seat.

notes.text: - **Peshwa as virtual ruler:** office hereditary from 1720; after **Shahu's death (1749)** the **Sangola agreement (1750)** made the Chhatrapati nominal – the king became a non-entity from **Balaji Baji Rao's** time; by 1750 a **confederacy presided over by the Peshwa** (A and R true, R explains A). Seat: **Poona** (Chhatrapati at Satara).

q: Who were the first Vaishnavite devotees in South India?
explanation: The Alvars (12 Vaishnava saints, 6th-9th c.) were the first Vaishnava devotees of South India. The Nayanars were Shaiva; the Virashaivas came later in Karnataka.

notes.text: - **First Vaishnava devotees of South India = Alvars** (APPSC G2 2000, AP History PYQ; HPSC 2012) – not Nayanars, Bhagavatas or Virashaivas.

q: The socio-religious movement led by Saint Ramanuja, which emphasized devotion to Lord Vishnu and advocated for social equality, had a significant impact on Andhra society. What was this movement called?
explanation: A movement of devotion to Vishnu that preached social equality is the Bhakti movement, which Ramanuja carried into Andhra. Arya Samaj (19th c.) and Lingayatism (Shaiva) are different movements.

notes.text: - **Ramanuja's movement in Andhra** (Vishnu devotion + social equality) = the **Bhakti movement** (APPSC 2022) – not Arya Samaj or Lingayatism.

q: Who propagated pushtimarga, a religion of grace?
explanation: Pushtimarga, the 'path of grace' centred on child Krishna (Shrinathji), was founded by Vallabhacharya; Chaitanya founded Gaudiya Vaishnavism and Vyasaraya was a Dvaita scholar.

notes.text: - **Pushtimarga = Vallabhacharya** (APPSC G1 2019, G1 PYQ); **Shuddhadvaita = Vallabhacharya** (UP UDA 2002) – he developed the views of **Vishnuswami**.

q: Who of the following leaders of the Bhakthi movement was greatly influenced by Islam?
explanation: Of the options, Ramananda (Ramanadhan) preached monotheism and the equality of all castes and took disciples like Kabir; this is the reading of him as influenced by Islam. Ramanuja and the Nayanars lived before Islam had any such influence, and Chaitanya's Krishna bhakti came from the Bhagavata tradition.

notes.text: - Liberal ideas that echo Islamic monotheism and equality → among the options **Ramananda is the leader "influenced by Islam"** (APPSC G2 2011) – not Ramanuja, the Nayanars or Chaitanya.

q: Yatis in Vaishnav tradition have to wear this
explanation: Sri Vaishnava ascetics (yatis) of Ramanuja's order carry the tridanda (triple staff), unlike the single staff of Advaita monks.

notes.text: - Sri Vaishnava ascetics (**yatis**) carry the **tridanda** (triple staff) (APPSC Endowment 2022).

q: Who made the Paancharatra Agama popular?
explanation: Ramanujacharya, following Yamunacharya, defended the Pancharatra Agama as Vedic and made it the basis of Sri Vaishnava temple worship; Madhva, Nimbarka and Ramadasu did not.

notes.text: - Made the **Pancharatra Agama** the basis of Sri Vaishnava temple worship (APPSC Endowment 2022).
